<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rcea-1c14ab08" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d6fcbecfc95c0ed0">If total entropy falls after RLVR, does the model necessarily have fewer correct strategies?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arcea">Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-09 · Southwest University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Less probability on errors, more predictable verifier outcomes, fewer realizations of the same strategy, and concentration across distinct valid strategies can all reduce entropy. Inspect the conditional distribution of valid strategies.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If two valid strategies still share valid-trajectory probability equally, the effective mode count stays at 2 even when all failed trajectories lose probability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09448">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2611.09448-rcea/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d6fcbecfc95c0ed0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rcea" data-paper-title="Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-00b0d44ac6c7a232">Why not report one effective mode when valid successes have zero probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arcea">Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-09 · Southwest University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An effective count of exp(0) = 1 means one mode holds all conditional probability. With no valid successes, that conditional distribution does not exist. Only its weighted entropy contribution is zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>When all probability belongs to failed trajectories, the mode term has zero weight. A reported count of 1 would falsely imply at least one valid strategy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09448">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2611.09448-rcea/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-00b0d44ac6c7a232">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rcea" data-paper-title="Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b6a13213bc039f6b">Why do trajectory entropy and outcome-conditioned mean token entropy use different formulas?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arcea">Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-09 · Southwest University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Trajectory entropy is Shannon entropy of complete paths. Its chain rule contains outcome entropy. Mean token entropy is a local statistic averaged along paths, so total expectation just weights the conditional means.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>When half the trajectories succeed, outcome entropy contributes log(2) nats to the trajectory decomposition. Do not add it again to the outcome-weighted token average.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09448">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2611.09448-rcea/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b6a13213bc039f6b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rcea" data-paper-title="Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae66013b52ab3feb">What happens to local covariance and actual entropy if every logit at one prefix receives the same increment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arcea">Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-09 · Southwest University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Covariance with a constant is zero, and a common shift leaves softmax unchanged. Both should give zero change, making this a useful negative control.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For logits (2, 0, -2) and increments (1, 1, 1), the prediction and finite difference are both 0. Absolute logit change is not entropy change.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与代码映射. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09448">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2611.09448-rcea/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae66013b52ab3feb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlid" data-paper-title="RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rlid-6c4a96d3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-535bebd40c60bf5c">How does a RLiD action differ fundamentally from an LLM writing an action command?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlid">RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>RLiD normalizes over compiled executable single-token menu labels and selects an action in one forward pass, without generating or parsing free text. Benefits depend on the menu and observation interface. It does not automatically preserve the extra computation provided by long reasoning, or guarantee stronger performance on every task.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: With only open and take in the menu, label B maps directly to take; free text might contain only an explanation. Legal output follows from an interface contract, not 100% task success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02455v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2611.02455-rlid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-535bebd40c60bf5c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlid" data-paper-title="RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1896ad1c56eb6817">Does RLiD&#x27;s variance theorem prove a newly trained LDM must beat a generative LLM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlid">RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Within one text policy, the identity marginalizes alternative wordings that map to the same action. Given that action, advantage must not depend on wording. It preserves expected updates and removes realization variance, not differences between model parameterizations or training runs, nor temporal-credit noise.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: open drawer and I should open drawer can be marginalized into one action. If reward separately values polite wording, advantage depends on wording and the assumption fails.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与代码映射. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02455v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2611.02455-rlid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1896ad1c56eb6817">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlid" data-paper-title="RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9651f0731d322a25">Is KL from uniform to the menu marginal equivalent to making every decision more random?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlid">RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It first averages microbatch action distributions within a menu group, then encourages that label marginal toward uniformity. Individual decisions can remain confident. Per-decision entropy instead encourages each row to spread out, changing the target. External calibration subtraction is another label-bias treatment with a separate update schedule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: Decisions near [1,0] and [0,1] average to [.5,.5], giving zero marginal KL despite low entropy in each row.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 结果、负控与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02455v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2611.02455-rlid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9651f0731d322a25">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlid" data-paper-title="RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-aacc956d8ee80eb3">Do executable menus and clipped PPO complete RLiD agent training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlid">RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Old-policy log-probabilities and advantages must come from actual external sampling, stay frozen, and align with the same menu. Local code supplies no LM, compiler, memory, GiGPO, or distillation. With mean-episode-length divided by each episode&#x27;s length as weights, average weighted decisions without arbitrarily dividing again by total weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: A two-step episode with .75 per step and a one-step episode with weight 1.5 both total 1.5. This checks weighting, not the paper&#x27;s 99.3% ALFWorld full-route result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 数据协议与代码映射, 结果、负控与边界, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02455v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2611.02455-rlid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aacc956d8ee80eb3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:moer" data-paper-title="MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-moer-39449a72" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5603dfb9948cf6c0">Why progressively shorten MOER expert prefixes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Amoer">MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · City University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Complete solutions limit exploration, but no guidance can be too hard. Shortening transfers more continuation to the student. If continuation fails, roll back to a verified complete expert trace rather than treating failure as demonstration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Give two steps, then one, leaving more of the derivation to the student.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30873v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.30873-moer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5603dfb9948cf6c0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:moer" data-paper-title="MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8338e49fb024a4f2">Why is a student continuation after an expert prefix still off-policy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Amoer">MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · City University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is conditional on a supplied prefix, not a complete sample from unguided student. MOER keeps successful guided traces and falls back to verified expert traces on failure, using distinct objectives. Expert data stay in training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Completing a proof after the teacher provides the key step is not reaching that state independently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30873v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.30873-moer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8338e49fb024a4f2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:moer" data-paper-title="MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ab9fbec477f9eb53">How does MOER distinguish native on-policy and guided trajectories?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Amoer">MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · City University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The whole guided trace is off-policy even if the student wrote the suffix, because its starting state was externally influenced. Use different objectives, not token authorship to reclassify the suffix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A student writing step three after two expert steps remains in the guided trace.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30873v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.30873-moer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ab9fbec477f9eb53">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:moer" data-paper-title="MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6db180f129af89fe">How can MOER&#x27;s off-policy ratio equal one forward yet have gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Amoer">MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · City University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The denominator is detached and numerator differentiable, so equal values do not cancel derivatives. Joint group advantages are not divided by SD; normalize over all valid response tokens, not extra mixture-weighted counts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A numerator divided by its detached copy is one, but differentiating numerator still changes loss.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30873v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.30873-moer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6db180f129af89fe">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cord" data-paper-title="CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-cord-0b4a5d25" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a09f25b1ef523765">Why does CORD select a protected objective first?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Acord">CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Adding conflicting task and teacher gradients can cancel them. The protected direction states whose first-order progress must not be harmed; modify the other minimally. It is a tradeoff.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Protecting task reward versus teacher imitation defines different projections.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29965v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.29965-cord/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a09f25b1ef523765">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cord" data-paper-title="CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1ebcba12aeca3711">Why project one gradient relative to a chosen protected gradient?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Acord">CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Minimally change the conflicting other vector to preserve the selected objective. Swapping protection changes updates. Conflict-only and always differ; project after full-batch accumulation. This is pre-optimizer first-order geometry, not guaranteed finite AdamW descent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Task reward and imitation may push a parameter oppositely; changing which is protected changes what survives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29965v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.29965-cord/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1ebcba12aeca3711">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cord" data-paper-title="CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-05b2cde4b0ffd64b">How do CORD conflict-only and always-project variants differ?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Acord">CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Conflict gating keeps helpful aligned components and projects only for negative dot product. Always projecting removes even helpful parallel components. The resulting direction is different; no finite adaptive-optimizer descent guarantee.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Aligned gradients add directly under conflict gating; always-project still removes a parallel component.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29965v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.29965-cord/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-05b2cde4b0ffd64b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cord" data-paper-title="CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-096a6edd2e82c442">Why aggregate a full CORD optimizer batch before projecting once?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Acord">CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Projection is nonlinear, so per-microbatch projection and summation usually differ. After fixed aggregation apply objective weight λ first. Skip projection if protected gradient is zero; λ=0 returns first objective direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Conflicts in two microbatches can cancel in the aggregate; early projection changes the result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29965v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.29965-cord/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-096a6edd2e82c442">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orl-diffusion" data-paper-title="On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-orl-diffusion-21689257" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7afac6883271e078">Why train ORL diffusion on its own induced residual contexts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorl-diffusion">On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Together AI / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The previous prediction creates the next residual and carries model errors at inference. Ideal residuals induce a state mismatch; online collection and replay expose encountered states.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A denoising step must see wrong prior probabilities to learn recovery from them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20687">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.20687-orl-diffusion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7afac6883271e078">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orl-diffusion" data-paper-title="On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fd0685fda98823c0">Why replay model-generated residual states instead of fixed residual inputs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorl-diffusion">On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Together AI / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Predictions become subsequent context and propagate errors. Fixed/ideal training can miss the model&#x27;s inference-state distribution. Online collection and exact replay with entropy contraction address this during training, not through final-output fixes. No local full training evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An early wrong token bias affects the next denoising step; perfect residuals may never teach this correction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20687">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.20687-orl-diffusion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fd0685fda98823c0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orl-diffusion" data-paper-title="On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8a6e93004eb1c371">How does ORL differ from smoothing outputs after inference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorl-diffusion">On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Together AI / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Postprocessing changes final outputs only. ORL feeds previous distributions into later model states and trains on them, including exact replay and entropy contraction; simple averaging is not equivalent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Averaging two answers doesn&#x27;t teach denoising from a mistaken previous state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20687">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.20687-orl-diffusion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8a6e93004eb1c371">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orl-diffusion" data-paper-title="On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-59fae2e103ec2ef6">Can the repository call an ORL adapter for residual traces?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorl-diffusion">On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Together AI / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Literature-only: no adapter, metrics or GPU receipt. Equations are explanatory; generic diffusion or a registry name does not implement online collection and exact replay.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Adding an evolve key cannot create the trajectory process.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20687">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.20687-orl-diffusion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-59fae2e103ec2ef6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ggpo" data-paper-title="Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-ggpo-409d30ac" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a1894bc05c764de">Why distinguish GGPO behavior and reference policies?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aggpo">Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Behavior generates the sampled data; reference anchors KL. They needn&#x27;t match. Refreshing reference changes the later objective without resampling old data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One frozen policy collects replies and another anchors deviation penalties.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20814v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.20814-ggpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a1894bc05c764de">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ggpo" data-paper-title="Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1f2cbda8035e076d">Why can&#x27;t GGPO behavior and reference be treated as the same role?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aggpo">Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Behavior is the sample source; reference defines KL-anchored Gibbs objective. Optimize adjusted log-mean-exp vs mean without extra behavior IS. Reference refresh cannot rewrite sampling provenance; filtered/normalized logs are not raw theorem quantities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A batch collected by an old policy remains old-policy data after changing the optimization anchor.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20814v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.20814-ggpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1f2cbda8035e076d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ggpo" data-paper-title="Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-63db0ed06b4206f6">How does GGPO&#x27;s Gibbs gap differ from learner/behavior importance weighting?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aggpo">Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Differentiate adjusted-reward log-mean-exp minus mean within groups. No extra learner/behavior ratio multiplies updates. Off-policy data alone do not justify adding one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Old-policy data do not imply every objective must use the same importance ratio.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20814v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.20814-ggpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-63db0ed06b4206f6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ggpo" data-paper-title="Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8ef00609abac4e8a">Why not backpropagate directly through clipped GGPO LME?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aggpo">Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compute frozen coefficients with clipped learner/reference ratios, then update original sequence logp. Backpropagating through clamp zeroes saturated gradients and changes the surrogate. Keep full-batch normalization/filtering.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clipping weight construction doesn&#x27;t remove saturated positions from learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20814v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.20814-ggpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8ef00609abac4e8a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tapo-trajectory" data-paper-title="Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-tapo-trajectory-36082418" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d2a704ecd94eafec">Why track prefix-state shift rather than only the current ratio in trajectory TAPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Atapo-trajectory">Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University AIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Small earlier shifts accumulate into later visitation changes. A current action ratio misses prior branching. Prefix geometric log-ratios supply trajectory context with tighter position-dependent bounds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A similar final-action ratio does not mean earlier branches left its state unchanged.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13020-tapo-trajectory/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d2a704ecd94eafec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tapo-trajectory" data-paper-title="Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-dbfc5a17598c40cf">Why stop gradient through TAPO&#x27;s prefix geometric ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Atapo-trajectory">Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University AIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The ratio measures state drift, but current credit should not backpropagate into all earlier tokens. Freeze the geometric weight and preserve the current log-probability gradient separately. This avoids cross-position gradients and length dilution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Adjust step ten for prefix drift without rewriting credit for steps one through nine.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13020-tapo-trajectory/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dbfc5a17598c40cf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tapo-trajectory" data-paper-title="Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-db3847d99823a9c8">How does prefix geometric mean differ from multiplying probability ratios?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Atapo-trajectory">Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University AIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Exponentiate average log ratio to limit extreme length scaling. This is a different estimator, not an equivalent numerically stable product.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Many small per-step shifts can create an extreme product while the geometric mean retains typical scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13020-tapo-trajectory/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-db3847d99823a9c8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tapo-trajectory" data-paper-title="Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b8acbe2f1744cbf8">How does TAPO prevent prefix weighting from dividing current-token gradients by position?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Atapo-trajectory">Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University AIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Detach the geometric ratio and multiply by current probability divided by its detached copy. Forward keeps the weight; backward follows only current action, without prior gradients or inverse-prefix dilution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Step ten can use ten-step context without automatically receiving one-tenth gradient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13020-tapo-trajectory/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b8acbe2f1744cbf8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gppo-framework" data-paper-title="Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-gppo-framework-a99015aa" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7e47d9d0de4b56de">What two independent choices define GPPO&#x27;s proximal updates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agppo-framework">Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University AIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Choose f-divergence geometry and its estimation topology. Combinations allow different ratio ranges; a common framework does not make instances train identically.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Different treatment of complement probability can change trust regions for the same divergence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13015">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13015-gppo-framework/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7e47d9d0de4b56de">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gppo-framework" data-paper-title="Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9f37ce2c9a7ea94c">Why can the same f-divergence give different trust regions with MC, atomic or binary estimation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agppo-framework">Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University AIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Topology decides how action and complement probabilities enter. Even fixed function/radius need not yield the same ratio interval. GPPO separates these choices and uses the resulting bounds. Preserve different KL forms instead of renaming GRPO.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Constraining only a rare action versus also the remaining mass can allow different changes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13015">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13015-gppo-framework/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9f37ce2c9a7ea94c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gppo-framework" data-paper-title="Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-418da2f4d66475da">Why are MC, atomic and binary topologies more than implementation details?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agppo-framework">Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University AIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They count sampled actions and unsampled complements differently, changing estimated divergence and admissible ratios. Name mappings establish no equivalence without the matching definitions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Binary accounts for one minus action probability, not just a renamed atomic result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13015">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13015-gppo-framework/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-418da2f4d66475da">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gppo-framework" data-paper-title="Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-21dcbebdc78ec1a6">Why expose literal KL and two-sided log separately in GPPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agppo-framework">Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University AIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Some algorithm mappings and printed formulas differ; keep both explicit rather than silently fix one. Ratios must be positive and binary complements valid; solve the selected trust region instead of copying PPO bounds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A configuration called KL that actually computes two-sided log obscures what was verified.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13015">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13015-gppo-framework/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-21dcbebdc78ec1a6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:zcpo" data-paper-title="When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-zcpo-1bf32735" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-bbc74cf447b9f8d5">Why put KL drift into ZCPO group coefficients rather than an independent loss?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Azcpo">When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A standalone KL can update policy with no reward distinction. Center relative KL and rewards into zero-sum coefficients for the existing surrogate and relative group credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal rewards should not trigger a training step merely because a separate KL exists.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.12161-zcpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bbc74cf447b9f8d5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:zcpo" data-paper-title="When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-16d59c38f113dc65">Why use zero-sum KL coefficients instead of adding KL loss?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Azcpo">When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent KL can update when reward gradients cancel or rewards tie. Center average conditional-KL drift with group rewards and feed the existing surrogate. Skip zero-scale/ineligible groups, including optimizer side effects, rather than returning zero loss and stepping.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>All rewards equal gives no relative signal; verify no optimizer update rather than rely on the logged loss.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.12161-zcpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16d59c38f113dc65">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:zcpo" data-paper-title="When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-65b69d8e4f98bf16">Can a sampled-token log ratio substitute for ZCPO conditional KL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Azcpo">When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Use full-vocabulary conditional KL, averaged along each response and centered across group. A sampled ratio is a different noisy estimator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A rare sampled token&#x27;s drift does not describe the entire conditional distribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.12161-zcpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-65b69d8e4f98bf16">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:zcpo" data-paper-title="When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3d89399c52763499">Why skip optimizer updates for all-equal rewards in ZCPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Azcpo">When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reward scale is zero, and AdamW decay may move parameters even with a zero loss. Skip the group/step; undersized groups also cannot form relative coefficients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Zero logged gradient plus weight decay can still alter the model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.12161-zcpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3d89399c52763499">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpening-tax" data-paper-title="Sharpening Tax in Post-Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-sharpening-tax-09653801" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b1670c70f32180f7">Why measure both first-attempt success and fixed-budget coverage in Sharpening Tax?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpening-tax">Sharpening Tax in Post-Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Training may raise probability of familiar successes while making other solutions or tasks unreachable. Fixed-budget coverage exposes this tradeoff.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One problem becomes usually correct while another never yields a correct sample, reducing coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01509-sharpening-tax/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b1670c70f32180f7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpening-tax" data-paper-title="Sharpening Tax in Post-Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7fe59e1e2e6de973">Why measure fixed-budget task coverage even when pass@1 improves?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpening-tax">Sharpening Tax in Post-Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sharper distributions hit familiar solutions more often but may lose rare solutions accessible with several draws. Compare base/post coverage under equal budget and adapt temperature by difficulty. First-hit accuracy, entropy and task coverage are not interchangeable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Better common-item answers can hide lost rare correct solutions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01509-sharpening-tax/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7fe59e1e2e6de973">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpening-tax" data-paper-title="Sharpening Tax in Post-Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4b1a6a6ef598e60f">How does posterior-conditioned temperature differ from uniformly raising temperature?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpening-tax">Sharpening Tax in Post-Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Allocate temperature by estimated difficulty to balance exploitation and coverage. Global heating treats all tasks alike. Bad estimates may misallocate, so recovery isn&#x27;t guaranteed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Mastered problems may need little exploration while difficult problems benefit from branching.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01509-sharpening-tax/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4b1a6a6ef598e60f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpening-tax" data-paper-title="Sharpening Tax in Post-Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cdbe2496774f9c56">Why hold K and task inputs fixed when computing Tax_K?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpening-tax">Sharpening Tax in Post-Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Coverage changes with samples and tasks. Match both and retain the sign of base minus post-training coverage. Local code is a metric only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Many base samples against one post-training sample confound the estimated tax.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01509-sharpening-tax/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cdbe2496774f9c56">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcpr" data-paper-title="RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rlcpr-dde5901c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f17b3c74251f3a07">Why not apply a uniform length penalty to all long replies in RLCPR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcpr">RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long reasoning can be necessary. Enable relative penalty only when all group replies are long and answer posteriors concentrated, where length may add little distinction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated explanation after agreement differs from exploring uncertain critical branches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01458-rlcpr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f17b3c74251f3a07">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcpr" data-paper-title="RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-524181a96eb45723">Why penalize relative length only if all answers are long and posteriors concentrated?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcpr">RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similar posteriors indicate limited distinction from reasoning length; widespread long replies support compressing redundant ones. Penalize relatively only after both gates. Equality and quantile rules matter; real entropy/posteriors must come from a model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Favor shorter among equally supported long replies, not a long reply that clearly increases answer support.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01458-rlcpr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-524181a96eb45723">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcpr" data-paper-title="RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-89ed669827603c39">Are RLCPR entropy strata and length gating the same choice?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcpr">RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Entropy strata shape examples before sampling. Length/posterior gates adjust rewards inside generated groups. Different inputs and stages, not one global length threshold.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Deciding which tasks to sample precedes checking whether current replies are all redundant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01458-rlcpr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-89ed669827603c39">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcpr" data-paper-title="RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
